title: Car Fleet
summary: Cars drive toward the same destination, `target` miles down a one-lane road. Car i starts at mile `position[i]` and drives at a constant `speed[i]` miles per hour. No car can pass another: a faster car that catches up with a slower one stays right behind it, and from then on they drive together as one fleet at the slower speed. Cars that meet exactly at the destination also count as one fleet. Return how many fleets arrive.

examples.explanation: Closest first: the car at 16 needs 2 hours and the car at 12 also 2, so they arrive together. The car at 10 needs 10 hours and leads a second fleet; the cars at 4 (8 hours) and 0 (4 hours) catch it.
Both cars need 3 hours, so the faster one catches the slower one right at the destination: one fleet.

constraints: All starting positions are different, and they come in no particular order

approaches.twist: Sort cars by position from the destination back; a car whose arrival time is not later than the fleet ahead joins it.
For each car, check every car ahead of it; it leads a fleet only if it arrives later than all of them.
approaches.note: Works, but comparing each car with every car ahead takes O(n²) time. Sorting by position lets one pass compare each car with the fleet just ahead.

signals.meaning: Order on the road never changes, so work from the car closest to the destination backward: each car only meets the fleet directly ahead of it.

signals.phrase: as one fleet at the slower speed
signals.meaning: A fleet arrives when its slowest car would. So a car that would arrive no later than the fleet ahead joins it; one that would arrive later starts a new fleet. Keep the fleets' arrival times on a stack.
The cars must be lined up by position first: sort them by position, closest to the destination first.

constraintReading: n can reach 10⁵, so comparing every car with every car ahead is about 5·10⁹ checks: O(n²) is out. Sorting the cars by position is O(n log n), and after that one pass compares each car with only the fleet just ahead. The sorted list and the stack of fleets take O(n) space.

hints.clarify: When do two cars become a fleet? When the one behind would reach the destination no later than the one ahead: it catches up on the way (or right at the end) and slows down. Try target = 10, cars at 6 (speed 2) and 2 (speed 4) by hand: the first needs 2 hours, the second 2 hours too, so they meet at the destination: one fleet. With the second car at speed 1 it needs 8 hours and arrives alone: two fleets.
hints.approach: Stack of fleets, built from the destination backward. Pair each position with its speed and sort by position, closest to the destination first. For each car, work out the time it would need on an empty road, (target − position) / speed. Compare it with the arrival time of the fleet just ahead, the top of the stack: if it's not later, the car catches that fleet and joins it, so nothing changes. If it's later, the car can't catch up, so it leads a new fleet: push its time. The answer is the number of times on the stack.
hints.whyNot: Simulating the cars hour by hour depends on the distances and needs care with cars that meet between whole hours. Comparing each car with every car ahead of it works, but it's O(n²). Sorting by speed instead of position loses the road order, and the order is what decides who blocks whom.

slots.setup: The cars as (position, speed) pairs sorted by position from the destination back, and an empty stack of fleet arrival times.
slots.loop: Visit the cars in that order, closest to the destination first.
slots.update: If the car's time is later than the time on top of the stack, push it: a new fleet. Otherwise skip the push: the car joins the fleet ahead, which keeps that fleet's (later) time.
slots.record: Work out the car's time to the destination on an empty road: (target − position) / speed.
slots.return: Return the size of the stack: one arrival time per fleet.

solution.explanation: Sorting n cars takes O(n log n), and the pass after it is O(n), so the time is O(n log n). The sorted list and the stack hold up to n entries: O(n) space. Only the top of the stack is ever read, because a fleet can only be caught by the cars right behind it; the times on the stack rise from bottom to top. A single variable holding the last fleet's time would give the same count, and the stack shows every fleet.

events.label: time
events.say: The car at mile {p} drives at {s}: on an empty road it needs ({target} − {p}) / {s} = {(target - p) / s:g} hours

events.label: join
events.say: {t:g} hours is not later than the fleet ahead ({stack[-1]:g} hours), so this car catches it and joins it

events.label: new fleet
events.say: No fleet is ahead of the car closest to the destination, so it leads the first fleet, arriving in {t:g} hours

events.label: new fleet
events.say: This car needs {t:g} hours, later than every fleet ahead, so it can't catch up: it leads a new fleet

events.label: return
events.say: Every car either joined a fleet or led one. Count the arrival times on the stack: {len(stack)}

predict.ask: Will this car catch the fleet ahead?
Will this car catch the fleet ahead?

related.relation: Also a stack whose values only rise or fall; there the stack holds days still waiting, here the arrival times of fleets.
Also sorts first so that one ordered pass can do the rest.
